Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ “We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.” Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. For the record: This story was corrected to reflect that Josh Newman was one of 27 state senators who approved the gas tax in 2017. Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ “We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.” Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.
According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement.
In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy.
In the case of a governor's recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting "yes" means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting "no" means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

You’ve probably received your ballot for the November election in the mail and are thinking about how you’re going to fill it out.

Yes, the editorial board knows the election is less than a month away, but we are deliberate in our evaluations so we can offer the most timely and thorough vetting possible of the candidates and the issues.
If we had rushed ahead with an endorsement in the race for San Francisco District 8 supervisor, it likely would have been published before candidate Manny Yekutiel dropped out after a second allegation of sexual assault against him (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/daniel-lurie-pulls-endorsement-from-manny-yekutiel-22457996.php).
With so many measures on the ballot, we also want to take the time needed to do deep reporting. Many of the state propositions are complex (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-election-propositions-endorsements-22422891.php) and not what they seem to be on the surface.
For example, Prop 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research that could help cure cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease. Who wouldn’t want that?

But as we dug deeper, we discovered that Prop 38 is, as we said in our endorsement (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php), “One of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.”
About half of Prop 38’s bond money — $4.2 billion — would go to a nonprofit medical research institute led by the billionaires who paid to put the measure on the ballot.
“It took weeks of digging for us to find out that the institute doesn’t even have a completed building,” said Editorial Page Editor Matthew Fleischer. “This measure is a scam. But it’s ahead in the polls because people don’t know the full set of facts.”
Whether or not you agree with our recommendations for how to vote, we want to present exhaustive reporting and the best analysis possible in our endorsements so you can make informed decisions.
So be patient! We’ll have the full slate of diligently researched pieces for you with plenty of time left to vote.

Proposition 5
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
When there is a recall under the current system, voters receive a ballot with two questions — should this official be recalled, and who should replace them? — along with a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority approves the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
Prop 5 would eliminate the question about who should be the replacement. But the measure would also allow recalled officials to run in the election held to replace them, which the editorial board found more than odd.

California ballots are out. Why hasn’t the Chronicle finished its endorsements?
By Harry Mok (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/harry-mok/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 8, 2026
Voters can submit their ballots at the Contra Costa County election offices in Martinez. The November ballot includes many complex state propositions.
Benjamin Fanjoy/For the S.F. Chronicle
You’ve probably received your ballot for the November election in the mail and are thinking about how you’re going to fill it out.
Maybe you’ve checked the roundup of the Chronicle editorial board endorsements (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements) for advice, but alas, many of the entries say, “Coming Soon.” What gives?
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Voter Guide: California and S.F. Bay Area election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-bay-area-voter-guide/)

Yes, the editorial board knows the election is less than a month away, but we are deliberate in our evaluations so we can offer the most timely and thorough vetting possible of the candidates and the issues.
If we had rushed ahead with an endorsement in the race for San Francisco District 8 supervisor, it likely would have been published before candidate Manny Yekutiel dropped out after a second allegation of sexual assault against him (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/daniel-lurie-pulls-endorsement-from-manny-yekutiel-22457996.php).
With so many measures on the ballot, we also want to take the time needed to do deep reporting. Many of the state propositions are complex (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-election-propositions-endorsements-22422891.php) and not what they seem to be on the surface.
For example, Prop 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research that could help cure cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease. Who wouldn’t want that?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But as we dug deeper, we discovered that Prop 38 is, as we said in our endorsement (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php), “One of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.”
About half of Prop 38’s bond money — $4.2 billion — would go to a nonprofit medical research institute led by the billionaires who paid to put the measure on the ballot.
“It took weeks of digging for us to find out that the institute doesn’t even have a completed building,” said Editorial Page Editor Matthew Fleischer. “This measure is a scam. But it’s ahead in the polls because people don’t know the full set of facts.”
Whether or not you agree with our recommendations for how to vote, we want to present exhaustive reporting and the best analysis possible in our endorsements so you can make informed decisions.
So be patient! We’ll have the full slate of diligently researched pieces for you with plenty of time left to vote.

Recent endorsements
Proposition 5
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
When there is a recall under the current system, voters receive a ballot with two questions — should this official be recalled, and who should replace them? — along with a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority approves the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
Prop 5 would eliminate the question about who should be the replacement. But the measure would also allow recalled officials to run in the election held to replace them, which the editorial board found more than odd.

S.F. District 4 supervisor
Voters in San Francisco’s Outer Sunset and Parkside neighborhoods, which have been embroiled in political discord the past two years over closing the Great Highway, are voting for a supervisor for the third time in two years.
Incumbent Alan Wong is running for reelection to a full term against two candidates he beat easily in a June special election to complete the term of former District 4 Supervisor Joel Engardio, who was recalled over his support for closing the Great Highway to cars.

Prop 5 would eliminate the question about who should be the replacement. But the measure would also allow recalled officials to run in the election held to replace them, which the editorial board found more than odd.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 20, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 11:17 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Break the 49ers' grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 20, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 11:17 AM PDT

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

content.thinking:
I'm sorting through what the measure would do: it would let a recalled official run in the special election to replace themselves, which current rules bar. The Chronicle's editorial board called that flaw bizarre, and I'm noting that several other boards, including the Mercury News and OC Register, have come out against it.

I'm checking the remaining editorial boards, and so far the Santa Cruz Sentinel and the Sacramento Bee are still unclear. I also have a PPIC poll from early September showing 59% No and 35% Yes, and I plan to read the editorials, the LAO analysis, and the measure's text next.

content.text: There are a lot of editorial positions, and some of them mention a provision that lets recalled officials run again. I'll read the key ones in full, along with the proposed text and the polling.

Voters can submit their ballots at the Contra Costa County election offices in Martinez. The November ballot includes many complex state propositions.

You’ve probably received your ballot for the November election in the mail and are thinking about how you’re going to fill it out.
Maybe you’ve checked the roundup of the Chronicle editorial board endorsements (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements) for advice, but alas, many of the entries say, “Coming Soon.” What gives?

Yes, the editorial board knows the election is less than a month away, but we are deliberate in our evaluations so we can offer the most timely and thorough vetting possible of the candidates and the issues.
If we had rushed ahead with an endorsement in the race for San Francisco District 8 supervisor, it likely would have been published before candidate Manny Yekutiel dropped out after a second allegation of sexual assault against him (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/daniel-lurie-pulls-endorsement-from-manny-yekutiel-22457996.php).
With so many measures on the ballot, we also want to take the time needed to do deep reporting. Many of the state propositions are complex (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-election-propositions-endorsements-22422891.php) and not what they seem to be on the surface.
For example, Prop 38 would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research that could help cure cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease. Who wouldn’t want that?

But as we dug deeper, we discovered that Prop 38 is, as we said in our endorsement (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php), “One of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.”
About half of Prop 38’s bond money — $4.2 billion — would go to a nonprofit medical research institute led by the billionaires who paid to put the measure on the ballot.
“It took weeks of digging for us to find out that the institute doesn’t even have a completed building,” said Editorial Page Editor Matthew Fleischer. “This measure is a scam. But it’s ahead in the polls because people don’t know the full set of facts.”
Whether or not you agree with our recommendations for how to vote, we want to present exhaustive reporting and the best analysis possible in our endorsements so you can make informed decisions.
So be patient! We’ll have the full slate of diligently researched pieces for you with plenty of time left to vote.

Proposition 5
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
When there is a recall under the current system, voters receive a ballot with two questions — should this official be recalled, and who should replace them? — along with a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority approves the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
Prop 5 would eliminate the question about who should be the replacement. But the measure would also allow recalled officials to run in the election held to replace them, which the editorial board found more than odd.
