Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.
According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement.
In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy.
In the case of a governor's recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting "yes" means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting "no" means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don't end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall.
With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it's the people's right to choose a governor's replacement.
They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.

Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.

It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov.

Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. # Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Voters get their say with Prop 5
California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5, which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled.
Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.
The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters.
It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom.
Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections.
However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions.

## How would it work?
If Prop.
5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
